name: 24LC256T-I_SN
title: 256 Kbit (32K x 8) I2C serial EEPROM
summary: A 256 Kbit EEPROM organised as 32,768 bytes, read and written over a two-wire I2C bus. Writes go in single bytes or in pages of up to 64 bytes, each finished by a self-timed cycle of 5 ms at most; reads may run sequentially through the whole array. Three address pins put up to eight parts on one bus, and a WP pin locks the array against writes. The 24LC256 runs from 2.5 V to 5.5 V at up to 400 kHz; the 24AA256 and 24FC256 run down to 1.7 V, the 24FC256 at up to 1 MHz.

operation.text: The device is always a slave on a two-wire bus. A master drives SCL, grants bus access and issues every Start and Stop; either side can transmit or receive, as the master decides.

The bus is idle when SDA and SCL are both high, and a transfer may only begin then. SDA may change only while SCL is low; SDA falling while SCL is high is a Start, and SDA rising while SCL is high is a Stop. Every command opens with a Start and every operation closes with a Stop. A bit is valid while SDA is steady through the SCL high time, one bit per clock.

After each byte the receiver pulls SDA low through a ninth clock pulse that the master supplies, and holds it low for the whole high time of that pulse. To end a read the master leaves the last byte unacknowledged; the device then releases SDA high so the master can send Stop. During an internal write cycle the device acknowledges nothing.
The master sets how many bytes pass between Start and Stop, with no limit, but in a write only the final 64 bytes are kept; earlier bytes are overwritten first-in, first-out.

The first byte after Start is the control byte: the code 1010, then chip select bits A2, A1, A0, then R/W (1 read, 0 write). The device answers only when the chip select bits match the levels on its A2, A1 and A0 pins, so up to eight can share a bus (two in the MSOP, whose A0 and A1 bits must be 0). For a write or address set, two address bytes follow, high byte first. Only A14 to A0 are used; the bit above A14 in the high byte is ignored.
A0, A1 and A2 must sit at VCC or VSS. They are usually wired to fixed levels; when a microcontroller drives them instead, they must reach their logic levels before the device is used.

The master sends the control byte with R/W = 0, the address high byte, the address low byte and one data byte, each acknowledged, then a Stop. The Stop starts the internal write cycle, during which the device does not acknowledge. After it the address counter points to the next location.

As a byte write, but the master may send up to 63 more data bytes before Stop. They collect in the 64-byte page buffer and are programmed together once Stop arrives. The lower six address bits count up after each byte; past 64 bytes they wrap and the earliest data is overwritten. Pages begin at multiples of 64, and a write that runs past the end of a page wraps to the start of the same page, overwriting what is there, so software must keep each page write inside one page.
A write of fewer than 64 bytes refreshes the rest of its page too, so the whole page goes through a write cycle; that is why endurance is rated per page.

With WP at VCC the whole array (0000-7FFF) is protected; with WP at VSS it is not. WP is read at the Stop of each write command, and changing it after that Stop does not affect the write in progress. A write sent while WP is high is acknowledged, but nothing is written, no write cycle starts, and the device is ready for the next command at once.

Because the device stays silent during a write cycle, the master can find the end of the cycle instead of waiting the full time. Right after the Stop that begins the write, it sends Start and a control byte with R/W = 0. No acknowledge means the cycle is still running, and the master repeats Start and control byte; an acknowledge means the cycle is done and the next read or write can follow.

The address counter holds the address after the last one accessed. A control byte with R/W = 1 makes the device acknowledge and send the byte at that address; the master does not acknowledge it and sends Stop.

To read from a chosen address, the master first sends a write control byte and the two address bytes, then, instead of data, a new Start and a control byte with R/W = 1. The address pointer is already loaded, so the device acknowledges and sends that byte; the master leaves it unacknowledged and sends Stop. The counter then points to the following address.

Started like a random or current address read, but the master acknowledges each byte and the device sends the next address in turn, so the whole array can be read in one pass. The last byte is left unacknowledged and followed by Stop. The pointer wraps from 7FFF to 0000. A sequential read does not cross from one device into the next on the bus.
SDA and SCL have Schmitt trigger inputs for noise rejection, and the output edge rate is controlled to avoid ground bounce.
On the DFN-S and TDFN the exposed pad may go to VSS or be left floating.
